The Nike Air Force 1 is one of the greatest, most iconic sneakers of all time, and back at the beginning of the millennium, they were having a moment. This iteration, dubbed the Nike Air Force 1 ’01, features a refined shape and material changes that reflect the styling from 2001.

Nike Air Force 1 ’01

Release Date: 07/01/2026

Price: $130

Sizing: Go down .5 size for perfect fit

Buy at StockX
  • Summary: The Nike Air Force 1 ’01 takes things back to the early 2000s, with high-quality leather and a refined shape on the uppers.

Traction

The Nike Air Force 1 ’01 features the classic radial Air Force 1 traction pattern. It still performs well to this day (though maybe not on the level of the Air Jordan 1) and it’s one of the most recognizable outsoles of all time. This pair features solid rubber, and if you’re looking to hoop in them, they’re durable enough for outdoor use as well.

Cushion

The Air Force 1 was notably the first Nike basketball shoe with Air in the midsole. The Nike Air Force 1 ’01 doesn’t change a thing; the rubber cupsole houses a Polyurethane wedge, which is where you’ll find a full-length Air unit. You won’t feel any compression underfoot, but what the Air Force 1 does offer is a neutral ride with more cushion than something like the Air Jordan 1 or a Nike Dunk, but with a thicker, less flexible midsole.

Upper

This is the area where you’ll notice the biggest changes from the Nike Air Force 1 ’01 to the Air Force 1 07, which is the model we’re used to seeing on shelves. This model has a slightly more refined, less boxy shape, with a different Swoosh and a leather tongue, compared to the nylon tongues on the 07 version.

The upper materials here are a welcome upgrade over typical Nike Air Force 1 offerings. Are they premium cuts of leather? Not really, but the leather is thicker than usual, and soft to the touch with a thin polyurethane coating. The uppers will wear nicely over time and crease the way a leather upper should.

Fit

The Nike Air Force 1 ’01 fits a bit large, so we recommend going down a half size for the best fit. The fit will continue to get better the more you wear them and the uppers stretch and mold to your foot shape. If you like having some extra wiggle room in your casual shoes, true to size will suit you just fine.

Nike Air Force 1 ’01 Summary

If you’re a fan of the Air Force 1, but not a fan of the material and build quality of the mass-produced Air Force 1s that Nike makes consistently available, the Nike Air Force 1 ’01 was made for you. The upper changes aren’t massive, but the real highlight of the shoe is the leather. It’s a noticeable upgrade from typical Air Force 1 quality, and it’ll look and feel just as good when it’s been worn into the ground as it does straight out of the box.

The only question is, do you need two pairs?

9/10
Total Score
Buy Nike Air Force 1 01

Disclosure

We purchased a pair of the Air Force 1 ’01 to facilitate this review. Nike had no involvement in this review, didn’t receive an advance look at it, and has not attempted to influence it.

The first Women’s Air Jordan is back for just the second time since their original release in 1998. Simply named the Air Jordan OG, they’re pretty much identical to the 2020 retro, which was a nearly perfect release in its own right (at least from a visual standpoint).

These have a strong resemblance to the Air Jordan 13, and the original pair actually had the same tech specs as the 13. While this retro looks similar to the original, the tech specs have changed, just like with the 2020 retro.

Air Jordan OG

Release Date: 06/20/2026

Price: $155

Sizing: True to size

Buy at Nike
  • Summary: The Air Jordan OG is a great looking sneaker with high-quality materials and a great fit. Downgraded cushion is its biggest drawback.

Traction

The Air Jordan OG outsole is unchanged from the 2020 retro and the original release. Solid rubber with a herringbone traction pattern is implemented across the outsole, similar to the Air Jordan 13. The Air Jordan OG essentially feels like a slimmed-down version of the 13.

On court, these are just as playable from a traction standpoint as they were 28 years ago. Solid rubber, herringbone, and lots of flex grooves will always be a winning combination.

Cushion

The cushion on the 1998 release of the Air Jordan OG featured a Phylon midsole with heel Air and forefoot Zoom Air. They were made with performance in mind, and even today, that’s a great cushion setup for basketball. This version features Zoom Air in the heel, but the forefoot is nothing but Phylon. While the downgrade in cushion tech is for sure disappointing, it’s pretty par for the course with Jordan Brand retros outside of the signature Air Jordan line.

Upper

The upper on the Air Jordan OG is largely similar to the original as well as the 2020 retro. It features white leather, which is high quality stuff, at least for Jordan Brand. The “quilted” leather panels, much like what’s on the Air Jordan 13, are an EVA-backed leather, and they feel great. The black mesh panels feel the same as on past models, and these feature white leather piping around the mesh, which is a change from the black piping on the originals.

One material change that was made from the 2020 retro is the material choice on the tongue – while those had a synthetic tongue, this pair uses leather, much like the originals did… well, kinda. The material at the top of the tongue, where the Jumpman logo is, feels like a cheap synthetic material. If you’re going to put actual leather on the tongue, why half-ass it?

The other real change when it comes to the upper is the color of the “W” emblem on the heel. It’s red on this colorway – on the 2020 pair, it was black, and on the originals, it was silver. I guess if you’re looking for an easy way to differentiate the three models, that’s an easy way to do it.

Fit

The Air Jordan OG fits true to size, and they feel great on foot. Whatever size you normally wear in Nike and Jordan products is what you should get with these.

Air Jordan OG Summary

The Air Jordan OG is a great looking shoe, and this retro version certainly does the original justice in that regard. Is it a bummer that these don’t have the forefoot Zoom Air that the originals had? Yeah, for sure. However, if you’re not planning on getting these for basketball, which we assume you’re not, then you’ll be more than pleased with the looks, materials, and comfortable fit that these offer.

8/10
Total Score
Buy Air Jordan OG

Disclosure

We purchased a pair of the Air Jordan OG to facilitate this review. Jordan Brand had no involvement in this review, didn’t receive an advance look at it, and has not attempted to influence it.

Chinese brand Volanti has entered the basketball world, and their debut hoop shoe, the Volanti Rocket Air, is an overall performance beast.

Volanti Rocket Air

Release Date: 05/2026

Price: $159 (use code WearTesters10 for 10% off)

Sizing: True to size

Buy Volanti Rocket Air
  • Summary: The Volanti Rocket Air is an awesome all-around hoop shoe, with excellent cushion, traction, and fit.

Pros

  • Outstanding traction
  • Top-tier cushion
  • Great fit and support

Cons

  • Lack of in-store availability

Traction

The Volanti Rocket Air has excellent traction. The outsole uses a classic herringbone pattern, and the rubber compound used is extremely grippy. Volanti describes the outsole as “ultra durable,” and we’d have to agree. This outsole will perform both indoors and outdoors.

Cushion

WOW. New brands usually don’t go this hard in the cushion department right off the bat. The Volanti Rocket Air uses V-Bounce foam throughout the midsole – V-Bounce is a supercritical foam, similar to what you’ll get from other Chinese brands, or adidas’ Boost foam. In the forefoot, there’s an “Oversized Quantum Nitrogen Air Unit.” What’s that? Essentially, it’s Volanti’s version of Zoom Air.

How does all of that feel underfoot? Incredible. It’s bouncy, low profile, and absorbs a bunch of impact. It’s easily one of the best cushion setups you can get right now. Oh, and there’s a carbon fiber spring plate as well, giving the midsole some structure and energy return.

Materials

The Volanti Rocket Air has a “Dragonfly Textured Knit” upper, which is a triple angle woven mesh material. It’s strong, and has a crispy feel to it, which suggests there’s some TPU woven in there as well. There’s also hot melt TPU material in high wear areas. It also offers some breathability, which is especially great for outdoor basketball. Overall, it’s an impressive upper that is relatively strong and durable for a knit material.

The tongue is thin, but it’s comfortable and has strategic padding to relieve lace pressure. The collar lining is a cats tongue material, which should aid in heel containment.

Fit

The Volanti Rocket Air fits true to size. Stay tuned for a full performance review for a complete breakdown of containment and fit on court.

Support

The Volanti Rocket Air has support features everywhere, in addition to the excellent fit. The base is flat and wide, with a lateral outrigger and a lateral TPU clip that runs from the midfoot to the forefoot for additional stability. There’s a small external heel counter along with a more substantial internal heel counter. The aforementioned carbon fiber spring plate offers plenty of torsion support along with snappiness.

Volanti Rocket Air Summary

The Volanti Rocket Air is not Volanti’s first performance shoe, but it is their first basketball sneaker, and it’s a crazy impressive feat. This is an excellent all-around sneaker – it’s very similar to the Li-Ning Gamma 2, and it comes in at just $159 retail.

In addition to being a great indoor shoe, the Volanti Rocket Air is one of the best outdoor options on the market today. The traction and upper materials are more than durable enough for outdoor use, and there’s enough cushion and ventilation to hold up outdoors as well.

Overall, the Volanti Rocket Air excels in every category, and the cushion might be the most impressive feature out of them all. If you’re looking for top-tier performance, this is a new hoop shoe brand that offers just that.

Use our code WearTesters10 for 10% off at checkout.

9/10
Total Score
Buy Volanti Rocket Air

Kevin Durant’s newest signature shoe is here, and it’s a big departure from his previous two models. Despite upgrades in cushion and fit, there’s one issue with the Nike KD 19‘s construction that holds them back.

Nike KD 19

Release Date: 06/13/2026

Price: $155

Sizing: True to size

Buy Nike KD 19
  • Summary: The Nike KD 19 features a bold, double-lasted design and an excellent cushion setup. Lack of flexibility makes them a tough sell.

Pros

  • Good traction
  • Bouncy, springy cushion setup
  • Fit and materials are better than other current Nike shoes

Cons

  • Lack of flexibility, especially in forefoot

Traction

The Nike KD 19 features a storytelling-based traction pattern that is reminiscent of the KD 4. The pattern is full of thunderbolts that blend the numbers 35 and 7, paying homage to the various jerseys Durant has worn throughout his career.

As far as performance goes, the traction is good, though on a dusty court, you’ll need to keep up with wiping the outsole. We would recommend that you keep these indoors.

Cushion

The Nike KD 19 features a double-lasted midsole, meaning the upper wraps around the midsole instead of sitting directly on top of it. This midsole is comprised of Cushlon 3.0 foam with full-length Zoom Strobel, making this the first KD model to feature Zoom Strobel since the 15. While the KD 17 and 18 had solid cushion setups, this is certainly an upgrade, at least when it comes to tech.

As for how it feels, this cushion setup is… good? Zoom Strobel and Cushlon 3.0 are a proven winning combo, but the shoe overall is pretty stiff, making this implementation feel much more muted than what we’ve gotten on models like the Air Jordan 40. Impact protection is top-tier, but that’s not all that matters when it comes to playability.

On foot, you can definitely feel some bounce, though if you’re able to break the shoe in, we figure you’ll feel that cushion setup even more. How long will it take to fully break these in? Well… you’ll have to stay tuned for a performance update for that.

Materials

The Nike KD 19 uppers are visually similar to other recent Nike models, particularly the GT Future. Thankfully, this molded synthetic upper material is far more forgiving than what’s on the GT Future (or the GT Cut 4, or the Book 2). It’s a soft, pliable vinyl material that makes up the entire upper.

The tongue is fully gusseted (attached to the inner lining of the shoe) and features tons of padding. It’s super comfortable on foot and you’ll feel zero lace pressure as a result- though if you’re looking for ventilation, these won’t give you much. The lacing system is internal, except for the top eyelet, which will help with lockdown and getting the fit just right.

Fit

The KD 19 fits true to size, and the fit is much nicer than what Nike has been putting on their shoes recently. They’re not as tapered in the toe area, though they are still a bit snug out of the box. After some wear, the materials break in and loosen up a bit.

One thing to complain about is that these are pretty stiff, especially in the forefoot area. You’ll have to put in some work to increase that forefoot flexibility. Straight out of the box, there’s some issues with heel fit due to that overall stiffness. This will get better the more you break the shoe in.

Support

The Nike KD 19 is a pretty substantial shoe overall, due to the materials used and overall construction. One positive aspect of that, from a support standpoint, is that they’re absolute TANKS. The downside is that they’re not very mobile. If you can put some work in, you’ll hopefully be able to loosen them up, but if you’re looking for a flexible shoe that will fluidly mimic the movement patterns of your foot, you’re not going to love these.

As far as support features, you have a sizable lateral outrigger to accompany the double-lasted upper. This gives a ton of lateral stability – your foot isn’t going over the footbed while in motion. There’s also an internal heel counter, though it doesn’t help with heel slip issues due to the shoe’s stiffness.

Nike KD 19 Summary

The Nike KD 19 makes improvements over previous KD models in terms of cushion, and props to Nike for giving us a molded upper that is soft and pliable. That being said, the KD 19 is still a stiff, clunky shoe overall. If you have the patience to break these in, and you’re a fan of more substantial shoes, you’ll enjoy the cushion, fit and traction. If you want something light and nimble, don’t bother.

7/10
Total Score
Buy SHOE

D’Angelo Russell’s latest signature shoe is a nice step up from the DLo 1. Coming in at just $119, how does the Way of Wade DLo 2 stack up against other models from the brand?

Way of Wade DLo 2

Release Date: 05/2026

Price: $119

Sizing: True to size, up 0.5 size for wide feet

Buy Way of Wade DLo 2
  • Summary: The Way of Wade DLo 2 offers well-rounded performance, with excellent traction and fit and full-length cushion, in a light, sleek profile.

Pros

  • Great traction
  • Balanced, full-length cushion
  • Excellent fit
  • Good blend of support and mobility

Cons

  • Materials are relatively cheap, though entirely functional

Traction

The Way of Wade DLo 2 has an unconventional outsole, but the traction performance is very good. The outsole contains what appears to be six different independent traction pods featuring a multidirectional pattern. Upon further inspection, you’ll see the outsole is actually one continuous piece of rubber, with large flex grooves separating the traction pods. This gives the outsole lots of flexibility and points of contact with the floor, but doesn’t compromise on durability.

Similar to other Way of Wade hoop shoes, the rubber compound used here is durable enough for outdoor use.

Cushion

The Way of Wade DLo 2 has a low-profile midsole setup, featuring Li-Ning’s BOOM foam implemented full-length, with Light Foam Ultra as the foam carrier. It’s not the brand’s top cushion available – that would be Super BOOM, which is offered in the Way of Wade 12, All City 14, and 808 5 Ultra.

Regular BOOM doesn’t have the insane bounce that Super BOOM has, but this setup is resilient and has a good blend of bounce and responsiveness. For $119, this cushion setup outperforms most, if not all, shoes in its price range.

Materials

The Way of Wade DLo 2 has an upper comprised of textiles and hot melt materials, along with some synthetic leather at the toe and the tongue. It’s a lightweight, breathable upper that requires basically no break-in time. Is it premium? No, but it’s functional and it feels nice on-foot.

Fit

The Way of Wade DLo 2 fits true to size. While Russell’s past shoes – the DLo 1 as well as the Ice Blood models – had painfully narrow fits, these are way more accommodating in comparison. They’re not quite wide-foot friendly, so if you usually size up, that’s probably your best bet here.

Containment is excellent, due to the close fit, as well as the Light Foam and TPU caging surrounding the foot all the way around the upper.

Support

The Way of Wade DLo 2 has plenty of support pieces in place, highlighted by Wade’s PROBAR LOC system, which consists of three TPU support pieces located in the arch, lateral forefoot and heel areas. This prevents over-twisting and gives the shoe structure. You also have an external heel counter as well as an internal heel counter, which work together to secure the back of the shoe.

The footbed rests within the tooling, which widens out in the forefoot for extra stability, while also having a rounded shape for mobility on lateral movements. Overall, the combination of support and mobility is one of the highlights of the DLo 2.

Way of Wade DLo 2 Summary

The Way of Wade DLo 2 is the light, fast shoe in Way of Wade’s current lineup (along with the Flash 2, though these are better overall). The great part is you still get some great cushion and support, while maintaining a sleek overall profile.

At $119 retail, the Way of Wade DLo 2 outperforms shoes with far higher retail price points from major brands, and provides a well-rounded performance package similar to Way of Wade’s higher-priced shoes. If you’re in the market for a quick, responsive sneaker, these are a great choice.

9/10
Total Score
Buy Way of Wade DLo 2

Disclosure

The shoe that was cemented into sneaker and basketball history when Vince Carter threw down the nastiest dunk of all time is back in retro form. The Nike Shox BB4 was part of Nike’s Alpha Project and designed by the legendary Eric Avar, and features one of Nike’s most divisive technologies: Shox.

Nike Shox BB4

Release Date: 06/26/2026

Price: $190

Sizing: True to size, up .5 size for wide feet

Buy at StockX
  • Summary: The Nike Shox BB4 Retro remains faithful to the original, with a sturdy construction and iconic Shox technology.

Traction

The Nike Shox BB4 has a simple traction setup – a full-length rubber outsole featuring herringbone in the forefoot and outlines of the Shox columns in the back. Herringbone is as tried-and-true as it gets for traction, so if you wanted to take these on court, you shouldn’t have any issues with the outsole.

Cushion

The Nike Shox BB4 was the first Nike basketball shoe to feature Shox technology. While Shox were marketed as being extremely bouncy, they’re really just kind of.. there.

The heel area is separate from the rest of the midsole – the TPU heel counter also acts as a chasse for the Shox columns, which are made of polyurethane. The polyurethane doesn’t compress too much due to its density, which kind of defeats the idea behind the Shox technology. The columns themselves are actually hollowed out, but still, the heel area of the shoe will only give you impact protection – not bounce. The Shox also raise the heel area to the point where there’s a noticeable heel-to-toe drop.

The rest of the midsole is comprised of Phylon foam with a forefoot Zoom Air unit. The midsole is double-lasted, meaning it’s housed within the upper. This is the exact same cushion setup that was featured on the original BB4.

Upper

The Nike Shox BB4 is the same as the original product. The white panels are made of a vinyl material that mimics leather, while the navy panels are a synthetic nubuck material. The tongue is made of the same vinyl as the other white panels on the upper. It’s perforated, allowing a small amount of airflow, and it sits below an internal lacing system. Overall, the materials aren’t premium, but they weren’t on this shoe’s original run either, so we aren’t complaining.

For branding, there’s the mini Swoosh on the heel counter, along with the five dots on the lateral side and over the toe box, representing Nike’s Alpha Project. You also have Nike Shox branding on the tongue, heel, and the insole.

Fit

The Nike Shox BB4 fit true to size, and if you have wide feet, you’ll likely want to order a half size up from your true size. The internal lacing system combined with the double-lasted construction will give you strong lockdown if you choose to take these on court.

Nike Shox BB4 2026 Retro Summary

This is a pretty faithful retro to the original, which is pretty cool for such an iconic shoe. The Nike Shox BB4 is still totally functional on court, though the double-lasted midsole combined with the Shox in the heel may make these too clunky for you, especially compared to modern hoop shoes. These have also always been heavy for a hoop shoe, even back when they first released. Still, if you want to own a piece of sneaker history, or if you’re a fan of Shox, you’ll certainly like how these turned out.

8/10
Total Score
Buy Nike Shox BB4 2026 Retro

Disclosure

We purchased a pair of the Nike Shox BB4 to facilitate this review. The company had no involvement in this review, didn’t receive an advance look at it, and has not attempted to influence it.

title.rendered: Nike Kobe 3 Low Protro Performance Review

content.rendered:
We at WearTesters usually prefer the low top version of a shoe over its high top counterpart, but the Nike Kobe 3 Low Protro may be the exception.

Nike Kobe 3 Low Protro

Release Date: 03/12/2026

Price: $180

Sizing: True to size

Buy Nike Kobe 3 Low Protro
  • Summary: The Nike Kobe 3 Low Protro is nearly identical to its high top counterpart, but a lack of containment makes these an inferior on-court option.

Pros

  • Top tier cushion
  • Breathability and flexibility
  • Looks awesome

Cons

  • Lack of lateral containment and support
  • Inconsistent traction with translucent outsole

Traction

The Nike Kobe 3 Low Protro uses the same exact traction pattern as the high, which is a slightly modified version of the original Kobe 3 traction pattern. Traction performance on the Kobe 3 Protro was great, so it should be the same here, right?

Wrong – the traction on these is inconsistent. There was more slipping and worse performance on dusty courts than the highs, and this is likely due to the rubber compound. This pair has a translucent rubber outsole, and Nike’s translucent rubber isn’t consistent performance-wise. If you’re able to get a pair with a solid rubber outsole, we’d recommend buying those, since the performance of the solid rubber outsole on the highs was excellent.

If you’re playing outdoors, this outsole will be durable enough for extended use, and the translucent outsole should work just fine in terms of performance.

Cushion

The Nike Kobe 3 Low Protro has the exact same cushion setup as the highs, and unlike the traction performance, these feel just as good as the highs do. The midsole is comprised of Cushlon 3.0 foam, and there’s a full length Zoom Strobel unit in there as well. It’s bouncy, smooth, and also housed within a rubber cupsole, which helps keep it stable. Overall, it’s one of the best cushion setups you can get.

One thing to note is that the footbed sits higher off the floor than other Nike basketball models, so if court feel is more of a priority than cushion for you, you may want to consider other options.

Materials

Not to sound like a broken record, but the materials on the Nike Kobe 3 Low Protro are, you guessed it, the same as what’s used on the highs. The upper uses a mesh build with rubberized netting layered over the top – this gives the upper some structure while maintaining airflow and flexibility. You also have a leather toe cap, with additional leather on the tongue and the back of the shoe.

The difference in materials from the lows to the highs comes solely from the collar height, which actually makes a difference in performance and support this time around. More on that in a second.

Fit

The Nike Kobe 3 Low Protro fits true to size, but there are issues with containment. Despite having the same upper construction as the highs, the difference in collar height makes a difference in terms of lockdown. Having extra lace loops and material to work with on the highs made the fit more customizable and secure, which led to better lockdown throughout the shoe (though it did become a bit restrictive around the ankle, which can be the downside of wearing a high top).

With these, I was never able to get sufficient lockdown in the heel or from a lateral perspective, so my foot felt like it was going to slide over the footbed on every movement. That’s a dealbreaker when it comes to fit.

Support

The Nike Kobe 3 Low Protro has plenty of support features, like a carbon fiber midfoot shank plate and a strong heel counter. Those things don’t matter, though, when the shoe has a sloppy fit. Those features are also present on the high tops, so if you want support, go with those.

Nike Kobe 3 Low Protro Summary

While the Nike Kobe 3 Low Protro is pretty much identical to the high top version of the shoe, with the exception of collar height, that difference in collar height makes a huge difference in lockdown. Outside of the fit, these have a lot of great features, particularly the cushion. There are a ton of great cushion setups from various brands out there, but when done right, it’s hard to beat full-length Zoom Air.

Overall, if you’re looking for a performance basketball shoe, opt for the high tops over these.

7/10
Total Score
Buy Nike Kobe 3 Low Protro

Disclosure

We purchased a pair of the Kobe 3 Low Protro to facilitate this review. Nike had no involvement in this review, didn’t receive an advance look at it, and has not attempted to influence it.

The latest Nike Street Tough (or S.T.) hoop shoe is the Nike ST Charge. It’s built for outdoor use, and it was originally released solely in China. This colorway is the first one to release Stateside, and it’s Cade Cunningham’s PE that he wore during the NBA Playoffs.

Nike ST Charge

Release Date: 05/20/2026

Price: $140

Sizing: True to size, narrow

Buy from Nike Buy from StockX
  • Summary: The Nike ST Charge features outdoor-specific features, like enhanced durability and cushion, but lack of flexibility holds them back on court.

Pros

  • Extremely durable outsole
  • Cushion is comfortable and responsive

Cons

  • Excessive rubber makes the shoe feel stiff on-foot
  • Not wide-foot friendly

Traction

The Nike ST Charge features XDR-X rubber, which seems like an updated version of their XDR (extra durable rubber). XDR is used on Nike basketball shoes catered towards outdoor hoopers, as well as the EP models that are released in Asia, where outdoor basketball is much more common.

This colorway uses translucent rubber on the entire outsole, using a traction pattern that resembles herringbone, providing both linear and lateral coverage. The rubber wraps all the way around the midsole, acting like a cupsole. This makes the shoe more durable, but it also adds weight to the shoe and decreases overall flexibility.

Cushion

Look, another Nike shoe with a drop-in midsole! The Nike ST Charge uses a Cushlon 3.0 drop-in with a bottom-loaded Zoom Turbo (or Articulated Zoom) unit in the forefoot, along with a small midfoot torsion plate. This cushion setup will provide adequate impact protection for most players, both indoors and outdoors, along with the familiar, responsive Nike Zoom bounce in the forefoot.

Is the midsole compatible with other Nike drop-in models, like the Kobe 8 or LeBron 11? Maybe – we’ll test the midsole out in different shoes and see for ourselves. It would be nice to see Nike make their drop-in system more universal, like what Serious Player Only does, where you can use any drop-in midsole across their entire lineup of drop-in shoes.

Materials

The Nike ST Charge has an upper featuring textiles and thick TPU yarns, which is mostly covered by a layer of what feels like rubber, which Nike is calling “Monster Skin,” attached to the cupsole. The tongue is breathable and comfortable, relieving lace pressure without any issues. The materials themselves aren’t anything too unusual, but the implementation is where things get a little complicated.

All that rubber on the upper makes the shoe feel notably clunky, especially given the shoe’s shape and flat tooling. Have you ever worn duck boots? It’s kind of like that. Hopefully they break in and provide more flex.

Fit

The Nike ST Charge fits true to size length-wise, but the fit is definitely snug. The amount of rubber wrapping around the upper also means these likely won’t break in or stretch much. Going up a half size would likely be necessary for wide footers, but that will likely compromise the rest of the fit, especially in the heel. If you’re not able to try these on in-store, it’s hard to recommend these for anyone who doesn’t have a normal or narrow foot shape.

Support

The Nike ST Charge has standard support features, like the midfoot shank and a flat base, to go along with the rubber wrapping that makes the shoe pretty stiff. While you’re not going to over twist the shoe or suffer from containment issues, the price you pay is restricting the foot’s natural movement and flexibility.

Will these break in and become more mobile on court? Maybe, and Cade Cunningham certainly doesn’t seem to have any issues, but making a shoe this stiff isn’t worth the added support that the excess rubber may provide. If you enjoy hoop shoes that are more restrictive and stiff, you may love these.

Nike ST Charge Summary

Nike’s latest outdoor hoop shoe checks a lot of boxes that outdoor hoopers need in their shoes, like durability, ventilation, cushion and support. However, the overall clunkiness makes the shoe feel less playable than we’d like. Break-in time may relieve some of that, but with plenty of other options on the market which give you all the outdoor-specific benefits while also being flexible, the ST Charge isn’t among our favorite outdoor basketball shoes.

7.5/10
Total Score

title.rendered: Nike LeBron NXXT Gen Future “By JuJu” Review

content.rendered:
The newest entry into the Nike LeBron NXXT Gen line has built up some considerable hype since the first images surfaced. The Nike LeBron NXXT Gen Future “By JuJu” is USC basketball star JuJu Watkins’ PE, and it’s a shoe that makes some interesting design choices.

Nike LeBron NXXT Gen Future “By JuJu”

Release Date: 05/27/26

Price: $170

Sizing: True to size

Buy Nike LeBron NXXT Gen Future by JuJu
  • Summary: The Nike LeBron NXXT Gen Future excels in traction and fit, with some interesting choices when it comes to the cushion setup.

Pros

  • Awesome traction
  • Synthetic leather feels like the real thing
  • React foam feels great underfoot
  • Great fit

Cons

  • Zoom pods in forefoot aren’t as flexible and responsive as other forms of Zoom
  • Heel cage may negatively impact stability

Traction

The Nike LeBron NXXT Gen Future has a no-frills traction setup, using a modified herringbone pattern across the entire outsole. This should provide excellent traction regardless of court condition. The rubber is translucent, which for Nike can be inconsistent performance-wise, but the outsole feels super grippy so far.

Are they durable enough for outdoor use? The rubber does feel fairly durable, so if you want to use them outdoors, it won’t be a bad option. However, at a $170 retail price, you can also find better value for an outdoor shoe elsewhere.

Cushion

The Nike LeBron NXXT Gen Future has a unique cushion setup, especially among Nike’s current lineup of basketball shoes. These have dual Zoom Air units in the forefoot, which you can see through the translucent outsole rubber. This Zoom setup isn’t our favorite, especially compared to a standard Zoom unit, or something like Zoom Turbo or Zoom Strobel. Using two Zoom pods next to one another makes the forefoot area feel less flexible, and there isn’t as much court feel as you’d normally expect from a Zoom-based cushion setup.

The rest of the midsole is made up of Nike’s React foam, and it’s super comfortable underfoot. In the heel, the foam is enclosed in a rubberized TPU cage, though it’s not what you would expect. Instead of the cage being layered directly over the outside of the foam, there’s a noticeable gap between the cage and the foam itself. It seems to go against the point of the cage, but we’ll have to wait and see what it means in regards to stability.

Materials

The Nike LeBron NXXT Gen Future “By JuJu” uses a mix of textured synthetic leather and screen mesh on the upper. The synthetic leather looks cool and it also feels like leather, so we’re okay with it not being the real thing.

Behind the screen mesh on the lateral side, the internal lining is completely separated from the outer layer. Once you lace the shoes up, the laces will connect the layers. The collar lining is quilted, which is a divisive choice performance-wise, but it definitely looks cool. You know what else looks cool? The jeweled Swoosh on top of that screen mesh.

Fit

The Nike LeBron NXXT Gen Future fits true to size, and the forefoot area doesn’t feel as toe-crushing as other recent Nike basketball models, which leads us to think these were built on a different last. Hopefully this translates to better performance and less discomfort on-court.

Support

The Nike LeBron NXXT Gen Future doesn’t have the profile of a conventionally supportive shoe. The base is relatively flat, but the footbed rests fairly high off the ground, which can impact stability. The aforementioned heel cage raises stability concerns as well, but until we take them for a nice spin on court, it’s hard to tell how it’s going to perform. There is an internal midfoot shank as well as a heel counter, so these don’t completely lack in support features. Stay tuned for more insight on support.

Nike LeBron NXXT Gen Future “By JuJu” Summary

The Nike LeBron NXXT Gen Future “By JuJu” is an awesome colorway on an interesting performance basketball shoe. The original NXXT Gen was an incredible performer, and while these feel way different, they have lots of potential on court. The Nike LeBron NXXT Gen Future retails for $170, which is pretty steep, so we’ll see if the performance lives up to the price.

Stay tuned for a full performance review on the Nike LeBron NXXT Gen Future.

8/10

title.rendered: Serious Player Only Player 1.5 Performance Review

content.rendered:
Serious Player Only has built an entire brand on offering a variety of drop-in midsole options for their shoes, taking the idea of a “System” started by Nike with the Kobe 7 and actually delivering on it. Their newest model, the Serious Player Only Player 1.5, is the best shoe from the brand so far.

Serious Player Only Player 1.5

Release Date: 05/02/2026

Price: $190

Sizing: True to size

Buy at Serious Player Only
  • Summary: The Serious Player Only Player 1.5 is an elite all-around performer on court, featuring an outstanding drop-in midsole and rock-solid support.

Pros

  • Traction is great
  • Outstanding cushion
  • Fit and lockdown
  • Excellent support

Cons

  • Drop-in midsole setup isn’t for everyone
  • Lack of in-store availability

Traction

The Serious Player Only Player 1.5 has an uber-aggressive traction setup, and it delivers on every court condition. The herringbone pattern covers the entire outsole, providing grip in all directions. If that wasn’t enough, the rubber compound used is very tacky. We had no issues with traction whatsoever. Oh, and the outsole is durable enough for outdoor use, too. Serious Player Only always delivers in the traction department, and these are no different.

Cushion

The Serious Player Only Player 1.5 uses a drop-in midsole system for its cushion, much like all of their other models. These come with the new Explosive 2.0 midsoles, which feature a PEBA-based foam, the same stuff used on super runners and marathon shoes (think ZoomX). This stuff is not only light, bouncy and comfortable, but also durable. It’s our favorite SPO midsole setup to date, but if you own any other SPO midsoles from other shoes, you can use them here as well. Of course, if you use an orthotic or aftermarket insole, you won’t be able to use them here (but you can use them in the Easy1).

One notable change made to the Explosive 2.0 midsole is that the sidewalls are far less prominent than on previous SPO midsoles. Those raised sidewalls caused the toe box area to be cramped for some, especially people with wider feet.

There’s also an extra piece of EVA foam in the heel that’s intended to make the heel-to-toe transition extra smooth, and it definitely does its job, especially compared to the Player 1 Plus, which simply had a cupsole without any extra EVA.

Materials

The materials on the Serious Player Only Player 1.5 are pretty similar to what’s on the Player 1 Plus – textiles, threading, and TPU threads, with hot melt material in high-wear areas. It’s a lightweight, breathable upper that’s also strong enough for hard movements and cuts. There’s also a TPU frame on the lateral side of the shoe for additional support.

In the back, the materials will depend on the colorway – the pink “Budapest” colorway features a synthetic microfiber, while the white colorway uses real patent leather, and the black colorway uses synthetic patent leather. Ultimately, they all do their job, so you won’t be disappointed no matter which colorway you choose.

The tongue is light, with Nike Torch-esque perforations for ventilation, and it effectively relieves lace pressure as well.

Fit

The Serious Player Only Player 1.5 fits true to size, and the forefoot area isn’t as narrow and toe-crushing as the Player 1 Plus. We’d recommend you get your normal size. Lockdown and containment are excellent all around.

Support

The support features on the Serious Player Only Player 1.5 are impressive, starting with the fit and containment. The base is flat and wide as well. There’s a carbon fiber heel counter, and the collar lining is a cat-tongue material, which is more abrasive on the way up than on the way down, so it helps prevent heel slippage.

These also have a carbon fiber midfoot shank, and along with the TPU frame on the lateral side of the shoe, provides excellent torsional support.

Serious Player Only Player 1.5 Summary

The Player 1.5 is the best shoe yet from Serious Player Only – meaningful refinements were made compared to the Player 1 Plus that result in a truly great shoe. SPO has done a nice job of listening to consumers and making the necessary adjustments to improve their products. These have everything – traction, cushion, fit and support. It’s the best shoe featuring a drop-in midsole construction on the market today, and SPO is doing the drop-in game the right way, offering tons of different midsole options.

9/10
